headline.en: DNA is life's instruction manual—information that tells cells what to build and how

universal_truth.en: Instructions persist better than artifacts; pass on the recipe, not just the dish

fun_facts.en: If you unraveled all the DNA in your body, it would stretch to the sun and back 600 times
You share 60% of your DNA with bananas—life uses the same basic code
DNA contains only four 'letters' (A, T, C, G) but encodes everything about you

discussion_questions.en: What 'code' runs your life—beliefs, habits, values?
How is information passed down in your family or organization?
What instructions have you inherited that you didn't choose?

script.en: You started as a single cell, yet that cell knew how to become you—every organ, every protein, every detail. How? DNA. It's the instruction manual: information that tells life what to build. Just four letters, encoding everything.

text.en: I want to learn something new

response.en: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

script.en: DNA is information that builds bodies. This idea—that life is information—has profound implications. What does it teach us?

prompt.en: What does life as information mean?

text.en: Life is ultimately about information transfer—what persists across generations is instructions, not bodies; the recipe outlasts any single dish

response.en: Yes. Your body will die, but your DNA pattern could continue for millions of years. Information is more durable than matter. The code persists; instances come and go.

text.en: DNA is just a molecule in cells

response.en: It's a molecule, but what makes it special is that it carries information...

script.en: DNA has only four letters: A, T, C, G. Yet their combinations encode every living thing. Simple rules, combined creatively, produce infinite complexity. Constraint enables rather than limits.

prompt.en: What's your first impression of "Four Letters, Infinite Combinations"?

text.en: This confirms what I already knew

response.en: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

script.en: DNA doesn't store a miniature human—it stores instructions for building one. The recipe, not the dish. Instructions are compact, copyable, and can build fresh instances indefinitely.

prompt.en: How does this connect to what you already know?

response.en: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

text.en: I need to think about this more

response.en: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

script.en: You run on code you didn't write—genetic, cultural, familial. Understanding your inherited instructions helps you see what's truly you and what you might consciously revise.

prompt.en: What surprises you most about this?

text.en: I never thought about it this way

response.en: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

script.en: Here's today's wisdom: Instructions persist better than artifacts. Pass on the recipe, not just the dish. Think in terms of information that can replicate.

prompt.en: What resonates most with you today?

response.en: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

script.en: That's Day 264. Tomorrow, we'll explore what you get from parents—heredity. Until then, consider what instructions run your life.

prompt.en: Before you go—what will you take from today?

response.en: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

title.en: Code Audit - What Instructions Run You?

learning_objective.en: Identify inherited and chosen operating instructions

activity.en: What 'code' runs your life—beliefs, assumptions, habits, values? Which did you inherit versus consciously choose? Understanding your programming is the first step to debugging or upgrading it.
